name: Von Restorff effect
statement: An item that differs from the others in a list is recalled better than the same item sitting in a list where nothing stands out.
meaning: The test is the isolation paradigm. One item in a list differs from the rest on some dimension, by material, colour, category or size, and memory for that isolate is compared with memory for the same item in a control list. Which control list is used decides what the comparison means. Against a homogeneous list, where every item is of one kind, the isolate wins by a wide margin. Against an unrelated list, where every item differs from every other, the isolate still wins, and that second comparison is the one that carries the theory. Two readings of the result exist and they are testable apart. Either isolation lifts the odd item above what it would otherwise reach, or the similarity of the surrounding items drags them down, or both happen at once. Von Restorff's own data show both, and her explanation favoured the drag.

origin.who: Hedwig von Restorff, working under Wolfgang Köhler
origin.note: The paper is her Berlin dissertation, published as pages 299 to 342 of volume 18 under the joint series title 'Analyse von Vorgängen im Spurenfeld'. MacLeod records that the work was done with Köhler and that she was awarded the doctorate magna cum laude at 27. No English translation has been published. A translation by Andrea Dorsch, commissioned by Hunt, has circulated on university web pages since the 1990s and is the version quoted here.

evidence: MacLeod tabulates nine main experiments from the dissertation with samples between 4 and 84. The first showed five lists of eight paired associates built from five kinds of material: nonsense syllables, numbers, letters, keyboard characters and colours. Four pairs in a list came from one kind, and the remaining four were each the only pair of their kind. Pairs appeared for 2 seconds, three times over, and recall followed a 6-minute conversation. Massed pairs came back at a little over 40%, isolated pairs at almost 80%. A control run over 22 subjects gave 189 hits from 440 for massed pairs against 328 from 440 for isolated ones. The experiment that carries the argument came later. Fifteen subjects saw three ten-item lists, one card every 1.5 seconds, then read a text for ten minutes and wrote down what they could recall. Two lists held nine syllables and one number, or the reverse, with the odd item in the second or third position. The third list held ten unrelated things: a number, a syllable, a colour, a letter, a word, a photograph, a symbol, a button, a punctuation mark and the name of a chemical compound. Massed items were recalled at 22%, the isolate at 70%, and the same critical items inside the unrelated list at 40%. Von Restorff placed the isolate early on purpose, writing that at the second and third positions the subjects 'could not know anything about the contents of the whole list', so the item 'was not perceived as unusual and was not particularly salient'.

replication.headline: Hunt repeated von Restorff's own early-isolate procedure with 40 undergraduates and recalled the isolate at .70 and .80, against .40 and .30 for the same item in unrelated control lists.
replication.detail: Hunt ran the design between subjects rather than within, so each participant saw one list, and he fixed the isolate in the second serial position rather than the second or third. Twenty participants took the isolation lists and 20 the unrelated lists. Recall of the critical item was .70 when a syllable sat among nine digits and .80 when a digit sat among nine syllables. The matched items in the unrelated lists came back at .40 and .30. Von Restorff's figures were .70 and .40. MacLeod, reviewing the literature in 2020, described the effect as clearly robust and readily replicable, and counted 236 citations of the 1933 paper in PsycInfo and 817 in Google Scholar. Robustness is not uniform across tests. Kamp and colleagues report that free recall shows the advantage reliably while recognition usually does not, which they call a contradiction of both intuition and existing memory theories. Across six experiments they obtained no recognition advantage under a standard multilist procedure unless recall was tested first, and recovered effects for recognition and source memory only after raising the number of observations per subject and controlling test order.

study.cite: Hunt, R. R. (1995). The subtlety of distinctiveness: What von Restorff really did. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2(1), 105-112.

limits: No meta-analysis of the isolation effect was located. Crossref, PubMed and general web search were used, and what came back was reviews and single studies. Wallace's 1965 review is behind a paywall and could not be read for this entry, so its content is reported as MacLeod describes it: three groupings of study design, a conclusion that isolation facilitates learning of the isolated item, and an admission that the theory remained controversial. The early-isolate result, which is the load-bearing part of Hunt's case, does not hold for every kind of contrast. Schmidt and Schmidt tested 84 students and found the usual advantage for a midlist isolate, .55 against .43 for the same item in a homogeneous list and .27 in an unrelated list, but no advantage for an early isolate defined by semantic category. Early conceptual isolates came back at .44 against .63 for the same items in homogeneous lists, an impairment rather than a gain, and their second experiment reproduced that impairment without the distracting task. An early advantage survived in the same paper when the contrast was a number among words or a word among numbers. Applied claims rest on thin evidence. Pick, Sweeney and Clay tested 60 undergraduates on lists of nine advertising slogans under incidental learning and found the effect for a distinctive high-quality slogan but not for a distinctive substandard one. No comparable experiment in interface design was located.
misreadings: The textbook picture, one odd item in the middle of a long list, appears once in her paper. Hunt counts a single experiment where she isolated one item midlist, and it was a recognition test, adopted because her earlier recognition lists with several isolates gave differences smaller than her recall lists had. Everything else used paired associates with four isolates in eight pairs, or a single isolate near the start. Her explanation also runs the other way from the popular one. MacLeod credits Hunt with the point that she treated the advantage as a cost to the massed items rather than a bonus for the isolate, and her own numbers carry both: 70% for the isolate against 40% for the same item in an unrelated list, and 22% for the massed items against that same 40%. Perceptual salience is not the mechanism she found, and it is not required for the effect. Hunt cites Pillsbury and Raush's 1943 report of a substantial isolation effect with the isolate in the first serial position, where no context yet exists to stand out from. She did not name the effect. MacLeod records that Jenkins and Postman still called it the isolation effect in 1948 and that Green attached her name to it in 1956. She was not a psychiatrist or a paediatrician, as Wikipedia's article on the effect describes her. MacLeod, working from Humboldt University archives, has her dismissed from the Psychological Institute in 1935, entering medical school, licensed in 1939, publishing a pharmacology dissertation in 1940 and practising as a family doctor in Freiburg until her death in 1962.

sources.text: von Restorff, H. (1933). Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld. Psychologische Forschung, 18, 299-342. The Crossref record carries her name alone, with the volume and pages the literature quotes.

Köhler, W., & von Restorff, H. An analysis of the processes in the trace field, translated by Andrea Dorsch. The unpublished English translation of the 1933 dissertation, hosted by the University of Texas at San Antonio, and the source of every quotation and figure attributed to von Restorff here.

Wallace, W. P. (1965). Review of the historical, empirical, and theoretical status of the von Restorff phenomenon. Psychological Bulletin, 63(6), 410-424. Paywalled, and reported here only as MacLeod describes it.
